about.body1: My professional interests lie at the intersection of clinical medicine, neuroscience and neurosurgery, public health, medical education, and health research. I am particularly interested in translating research evidence into practical solutions that improve patient care and strengthen healthcare systems.
about.body2: Alongside my clinical training, I contribute to research projects, scientific writing, research training, and academic initiatives. Through the Haj Malik Research Group and the Abou-Aloloum Centre for Medical Education and Research, I work to support young researchers and promote a stronger culture of evidence-based medicine and scientific inquiry.

posts.title: Why Are Health Professions Students Struggling to Conduct Research
posts.excerpt:
A national study of 874 health professions students exploring barriers to research and training needs. 
auothers: Elalim mohamed, MBBS
Asma Mohamed, medical student
Rogia Mohamed, medical student
Rayan Ahmed, medical student
Tasneem Hamza, medical student
Thaqeb Gafar, medical student
posts.body:
Medical and health professions students are often encouraged to participate in research, but having an interest in research does not always mean having the opportunity or the skills to conduct it successfully.



So, what makes research difficult for students?



A national cross-sectional study conducted among 874 health professions students in Sudan explored this question by examining the personal, educational, institutional, and resource-related barriers that affect student research participation.



\## What did the study find?



The findings show that the problem is not simply a lack of motivation.



The most frequently reported personal barriers were academic workload (33.1%), difficulty understanding research concepts (30.8%), limited time (22.5%), and lack of confidence (13.6%).



These findings suggest that many students face competing academic demands while simultaneously trying to develop research skills.



\## Access to research resources matters



One of the most important findings was the widespread difficulty accessing research resources.



Overall, 60.8% of students reported restricted access to scientific literature and research-related resources.



Limited access to scientific databases, statistical tools, research materials, and other resources can make it difficult for students to move from an initial research idea to a completed project.



Importantly, access to research resources was also the strongest independent predictor of experiencing high perceived research barriers.



Students who reported difficulty accessing research resources had more than twice the odds of experiencing substantial research barriers compared with those who reported adequate access (aOR = 2.15, 95% CI: 1.59–2.91, p < 0.001).



\## What do students need to learn?



The study also examined the research competencies students considered most important for their training.



The leading priorities were:



\- Scientific manuscript writing (26.1%)

\- Research project management (25.9%)

\- Primary data collection (24.7%)

\- Statistical analysis (23.3%)



This is an important distinction.



Students do not only need to learn the theory of research methodology. They need practical skills that allow them to plan a study, collect and analyze data, communicate findings, and ultimately contribute to scientific literature.



\## Research barriers differ across academic stages



The challenges were not the same for all students.



Pre-clinical students primarily reported difficulties related to understanding research concepts and methodology.



Clinical undergraduate students were more affected by clinical schedules and time constraints.



Postgraduate students more frequently identified barriers related to software accessibility and research funding.



This suggests that research education should evolve with students' academic progression rather than relying on a single research-methodology course for everyone.



\## Previous research failure can matter



Previous unsuccessful research experiences were also associated with higher perceived research barriers.



Students who had experienced previous research failure or major hurdles had higher odds of reporting substantial barriers (aOR = 1.83, 95% CI: 1.31–2.56, p < 0.001).



This highlights the importance of mentorship.



A difficult first research experience should not become the point at which a student disengages from research. Structured supervision, constructive feedback, and practical guidance may help students turn early difficulties into learning experiences.



\## What does this mean for Sudan?



Sudan has a large and potentially valuable health research workforce in training.



Medical, dental, pharmacy, nursing, public health, laboratory, physiotherapy, radiology, and other health professions students represent an important foundation for the country's future research capacity.



However, research capacity cannot be built through student motivation alone.



Universities and training institutions need to provide:



\- Structured and longitudinal research curricula

\- Accessible scientific literature and research resources

\- Practical training in statistics and data analysis

\- Research mentorship and supervision

\- Protected time for research activities

\- Opportunities to present and publish research findings



\## From research education to research culture



The broader lesson is that students should not simply be told to "do research."



They should be given a clear pathway through the entire research process:



Question → Protocol → Ethics → Data → Analysis → Manuscript → Publication



When students receive the skills, mentorship, resources, and institutional support required to complete this pathway, research can become more than an academic requirement.



It can become part of the culture of health professions education.



\## The bigger lesson



The findings from Sudan highlight a challenge that may be relevant to many health professions students in low- and middle-income settings.



Research potential exists, but potential alone is not enough.



Students need access, mentorship, practical skills, protected time, and supportive institutions.



Building research capacity among students is therefore not only an investment in academic productivity.



It is an investment in the future health research workforce.



\## About the Study



Barriers and Research Training Needs among Health Professions Students in Sudan: A National Cross-Sectional Study.



A national cross-sectional online survey of 874 undergraduate and postgraduate health professions students from public and private universities in Sudan, conducted between November 2025 and May 2026.



The study was designed to identify major barriers to research participation, priority research training needs, and independent predictors of high perceived research barriers.



Read the full study:



https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22308551
